paragraphs.text: 14.40. Applications to single appeal judges
paragraphs.heading: Part 14. Appeals

sentences.text: Applications to single appeal judges

paragraphs.text: (1) Subject to Subdivision 3, an application to a single appeal judge must be made by filing (a) an application that meets the requirements of rule 14.53, (b) any accompanying affidavit, if required, (c) other material to be relied on, even if previously filed, and (d) a memorandum of argument that meets the requirements of rule 14.54. (2) Subject to rule 6.4 and rule 14.44, the applicant must serve a filed copy of the application and other materials on every other party to the appeal at least 10 days before the application is scheduled to be heard. Alta. Reg. 41/2014, s. 4; 85/2016, s. 1(11); 61/2023, s. 20

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.40:1 Rule 14.40 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.40. In Sobeys West Inc. v. Edmonton (City), 2015 ABCA 32, Justice Slatter gave the following directions regarding filing deadlines: 15 During the preparation for the hearing of this application, issues arose with respect to the filing deadlines under the new Rules, and the parties requested some direction. In order to reduce delay involved in the hearing of applications, time limits in the new Rules have been slightly truncated and varied. With respect to applications to single judges, the Rules now provide: R. 14.40(2) Subject to rule 6.4 [applications without notice] and rule 14.44 [applications for permission to appeal], the applicant must file and serve one additional copy of the application and other materials on every other party to the appeal at least 10 days before the application is scheduled to be heard. R. 14.41 The respondent to an application to a single appeal judge must, at least 5 days before the scheduled hearing of the application [file its response, as specified]. Rule 14.44 provides that an application for permission to appeal must also be filed within the applicable time limitation for appealing. 16 Single appeal judges hear applications in both Edmonton and Calgary every week (in the summer sometimes by video conference) on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays. Counting back the 10 days required by R. 14.40(2) and the 5 days required by R. 14.41 yields the following deadlines: Applicant	Respondent Tuesday hearings	Saturday 1 week before	previous Thursday Wednesday hearings	Sunday 1 week before	previous Friday Thursday hearings	Monday 1 week before	previous Saturday These dates are arrived at through the application of R. 13.3 and the accompanying Information Note: • Counting days • 13.3 When counting to or from an event or activity in days, the date on which the event or activity occurs is not counted. Information note • The basic rule can be illustrated as follows: • Counting forwards… • Counting backwards • Rule 3.9 [Service of originating application and evidence] requires certain documents to be filed and served on parties 10 days or more before the date scheduled for hearing the application. • If the scheduled date is May 15, the materials must be filed and served on or before May 5. The day of the event—the scheduled hearing day—is not counted. … There is no longer any use of the expressions “clear days” or “business days”. 17 Some of the identified deadlines fall on weekends, which invokes the provisions of the Interpretation Act, RSA 2000 c. I-8, s. 22(1) and (2): • Computation of time • 22(1) If in an enactment the time limited for the doing of a thing expires or falls on a holiday, the thing may be done on the day next following that is not a holiday. • (2) If in an enactment the time limited for registration or filing of an instrument, or for the doing of anything, expires or falls on a day on which the office or place in which the instrument or thing is required to be registered, filed or done is not open during its regular hours of business, the instrument or thing may be registered, filed or done on the day next following on which the office or place is open. … • (9) For the purpose of construing a reference in an enactment to a specified age expressed as a number of years, a person is deemed to have attained the specified age at the beginning of the relevant anniversary of the day of the person's birth. It is worth emphasizing that R. 1.8(b) provides that the balance of s. 22 of the Interpretation Act does not apply to the Rules of Court. In accordance with the provisions that do apply, when a deadline falls on a weekend, the litigant has until the following Monday to comply. 18 Failure to meet the deadlines in R. 14.40(2) and R. 14.41 has various consequences. Rule 14.90(1)(a)(i) contains a presumption that no costs are available for a late step. The Registry or the presiding judge may decline to set down a matter that has missed the deadline, depending on the number of matters scheduled that week and other considerations. Late filing by a respondent will not be allowed to prejudice an applicant: R. 1.5(4). Extreme cases of missed deadlines can result in appeals or applications being struck. 19 Litigants before the Court should, however, be aware that there is another meaning of “lateness” in this context. The Registry will deliver the application materials for any particular week to the presiding judge before some of these formal deadlines are reached. Documents filed after that date are “late”, in the sense that the rest of the material will already have been sent to the judge. While “last minute” filings will not be subject to the consequences mentioned in para. 18, lateness in filing may require an adjournment of the hearing into the future. Whether that is necessary depends on a number of factors, including the complexity of the application, the volume of material, the number of applications set down that week, and the other responsibilities of the presiding judge. Prudent counsel will file early, and certainly will not wait until the Monday after the weekend to file documents.

sentences.text: Application for permission to appeal

paragraphs.text: (1) An application for permission to appeal must comply with rules 14.5(2) and 14.40 and (a) must be filed and served and must be returnable within the period specified in any enactment or these rules, or (b) if there is no time for filing permission to appeal specified in any enactment or these rules, must be filed and served within the time for filing appeals set out in rule 14.8. (3) Applications to preserve a time limitation may be brought on the notice a single appeal judge directs. Alta. Reg. 41/2014, s. 4; 128/2015, s. 14

paragraphs.text: 14.45. Application to admit new evidence
paragraphs.heading: Part 14. Appeals

sentences.text: Application to admit new evidence

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.45:1 Rule 14.45—New Evidence See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.45. In Fougere v. The King's University, 2023 ABCA 374, Justice Fagnan said: [5] Under r 14.45(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010, an application to admit new evidence on appeal must be filed and served prior to the applicant's factum being filed. An applicant seeking to file a late application to admit such evidence must seek permission to file. [6] In P & C Lawfirm Management Inc v Sabourin, 2020 ABCA 285 (single judge), paras 11-12, this Court applied the test for leave to file a late application for new evidence under former r 516.2. In deciding whether to grant permission, the Court considered factors including the reason for the late filing, the effect of the late filing on the appeal proper, and whether the application for fresh evidence has a reasonable prospect of success or is prima facie meritorious: P & C, para 12, citing R v Gendreau, 2011 ABCA 256, para 32. [7] The threshold for granting leave is low: P & C, paras 12, 15, citing Belland v Belland, 2008 ABCA 226 (single judge), para 6. This Court has denied leave where the proposed additional evidence was only marginally relevant or material (Gendreau, para 33), where it was irrelevant (Belland, para 6), and where it was not even arguably probative (Stoddard v Montague, 2006 ABCA 28 (single judge), para 13). …. [10] The Court must also consider whether the proposed application has a reasonable prospect of success. In deciding whether to admit additional evidence on appeal, the Court applies the four-part test from Palmer v The Queen, 1979 CanLII 8 (SCC), [1980] 1 SCR 759, 775. The evidence generally should not be admitted if it could have been obtained for the hearing through due diligence. The evidence must be relevant in the sense that it relates to a potentially decisive issue in the trial and must be reasonably capable of belief. Finally, it must be such that it could have reasonably affected the result of the hearing. …. [12] It is reasonable to conclude that the proposed evidence would have been available to put before the chambers judge had the applicant acted with due diligence. While due diligence is not a condition precedent, failure to act with due diligence will generally foreclose the admission of fresh evidence on appeal: Barendregt v Grebliunas, 2022 SCC 22, paras 44, 61; Sunridge Nissan Inc v McRuer, 2023 ABCA 128, para 17.

paragraphs.text: 14.46. Application to reconsider a previous decision
paragraphs.heading: Part 14. Appeals

sentences.text: Application to reconsider a previous decision

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.46:1 Rule 14.46 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.46. In Lawrence v. Alberta (Director of Safe Roads), 2023 ABCA 271, 2023 CarswellAlta 2484, the Court set out the test for reconsideration of a previous decision: [14] This Court recently discussed the test for reconsideration of a decision in Peters v Atchooay, 2021 ABCA 237. As those reasons note, the function of the court on an application to reconsider is not to determine whether the previous case was “wrongly decided; ... only... to determine whether [it] should be reconsidered”: AC and JF v Alberta, 2020 ABCA 251, para 5; Edmonton (Police Service) v Deluca, 2020 ABCA 31, para 6, 97 Alta LR (6th) 291. As a general rule, leave to reconsider a binding precedent “will be granted in very limited circumstances”: R v Effert, 2010 ABCA 144, para 5, 26 Alta LR (5th) 96; Deluca, para 8. The policy considerations for this are readily apparent and are rooted in the need for certainty and stability of the trial process, finality in litigation, and judicial economy: Effert, para 5. [15] The factors relevant to assessing whether leave should be granted include: i. the age of the decision; ii. whether the decision has created settled expectations or resulted in other cases being settled or decided in a particular way; iii. treatment of the issue by other appeal courts; iv. whether some binding statute or authority has been overlooked; v. whether the decision has “some simple, obvious, demonstrable flaw”; and vi. whether the decision was a memorandum of judgment delivered from the bench or a reserved, circulated one. Deluca, para 8; McAllister v Calgary (City), 2012 ABCA 346, para 9, 69 Alta LR (5th) 242; Effert, para 5.

sentences.text: Application to restore an appeal

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.47:1 Rule 14.47 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.47. In Holden v. Holden, 2022 ABCA 341, 2022 CarswellAlta 2995, Justice Wakeling said: [37] Rule 14.47(a) of the Alberta Rules of Court stipulates that a restoration application “must be filed and served as soon as reasonably possible”. This is the case whether an appeal is a standard appeal or a fast-track appeal. [38] No other Canadian jurisdiction has this feature in its civil appeal procedure rules. [39] The same is true for other common law jurisdictions. [40] The “as soon as reasonably possible” requirement came into effect on March 17, 2020. sentences.text: An application to stay proceedings or enforcement of a decision pending appeal may be made
(a) to the judge who made that decision, or
(b) to a single appeal judge, whether or not the application was made to the judge who made the decision, and whether or not that application was granted or dismissed.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.48:1 Rule 14.48 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.48. 1. Test for a stay In Knelsen Sand & Gravel Ltd. v. Harco Enterprises Ltd., 2021 ABCA 362, 2021 CarswellAlta 2716, Justice Wakeling gave this very helpful summary of the law (footnotes omitted): [38] The standard stay test has three components. [39] First, does the applicant's claim present a serious issue to be tried, or is it frivolous, vexatious, baseless, hopeless, not arguable or has extremely low prospects of success? [40] Second, would the applicant suffer irreparable harm if relief is not granted, or could a subsequent remedy, such as a damages order, adequately compensate the applicant? [41] Third, would the applicant suffer greater harm than the respondent if relief were denied, or would the harm to the respondent from granting the application exceed it? [42] A court must consider the consequences of granting or refusing a stay of execution of a judgment and ascertain whose interests should be put at risk. An applicant may allege that it needs the funds to prosecute an appeal or that it is unlikely the respondent will repay to the applicant a sum paid under a judgment subsequently reversed on appeal. The respondent, on the other hand, may claim that the passage of time associated with a stay may reduce to an unacceptable degree the likelihood it will be able to enforce its judgment if the applicant's appeal is dismissed. Or the respondent may assert, like the applicant, that it needs the money to retain counsel to defend the judgement under appeal. “[T]he essential question is whether there is a risk of injustice to one or other or both parties if it grants or refuses a stay.” [43] An applicant who satisfies all three components is entitled to its relief unless the “applicant has not applied promptly for relief or other deficiencies equity traditionally recognized exist”. An applicant who fails to pass any one component is not entitled to relief. [44] Irreparable harm is typically viewed as harm that cannot be quantified in monetary terms. But back in 1994 Justices Sopinka and Cory opined that it can also be harm that cannot be cured because the applicant could not collect money from the respondent. The irreparable harm inquiry must reflect the context—the applicant seeks relief from having to pay a money judgment. [45] Most of the time a judgment debtor will stumble at this hurdle. A judgment-debtor applicant who pays a judgment creditor before a successful appeal occurs generally still has a viable and adequate remedy—sue the judgment creditor for the return of the money paid under a judgment that has been vacated or ask the appeal court reversing the judgment to order the respondent to repay the money unjustly received. [46] But circumstances may exist where having to pay out a money judgment can cause the applicant irreparable harm—for example, if the applicant would be unable to recover those amounts should it be successful on appeal, or if making the payment would cause the applicant harm that could not be monetarily quantified, such as putting it out of business. [47] An applicant who can demonstrate that there is a reasonable prospect the respondent will not be able to repay the judgment following a successful appeal if a stay is not granted, provided the respondent cannot establish that it has both the ability and intention to repay it, has made out irreparable harm. [48] The court may vitiate the harm arising from concerns about payment by ordering a party to give an undertaking and post security into court as a condition of either granting or refusing the stay. [49] This is somewhat similar to the undertakings required of an applicant upon obtaining an interlocutory injunction. Undertakings as to damages arising from a stay do not appear to be usual notwithstanding that, in effect, a stay of execution and injunction may well share similar features. In Venini v. Venini, 2023 ABKB 601, Justice Marion gave this summary of the applicable principles: [8] The test for determining whether the appeal is arguable or not has a low threshold….It does not require an examination of the merits of the case, but rather simply involves an assessment of whether the appeal is frivolous or vexatious…. …. [13] …irreparable harm usually must be that of the applicant and not potential harm to third parties or entities without legal standing…. …. [15] Further, evidence of irreparable harm must be clear and not speculative…. …. C. Does the Balance of Convenience Support a Stay? [28] At this stage, the court must consider which of the parties will suffer greater harm from the granting or refusal of the stay pending the appeal….The court must assess the severity of the harm and identify the party that should not be ordered to endure that adversity associated with either granting or dismissing the application because it exceeds that [which] the other party will experience…. 2. Effect of a stay In Denis v. Sauvageau, 2022 ABCA 166, 2022 CarswellAlta 1158, Khullar, J.A. discussed the effect of a stay of proceedings. What is being stayed? Her Ladyship said: [13] The application is brought under r 14.48(b) of the Rules of Court which provides that “[a] n application to stay proceedings or enforcement of a decision pending appeal may be made … to a single appeal judge …” (emphasis added). [14] A preliminary issue is that it appears that Mr. Denis is asking this Court to stay two different things. First, he asks the Court to stay the finding of contempt pending his appeal. Second, he wants to stay the proceedings so that the trial court will not address sanction or costs while he appeals the finding of contempt. [15] A stay of proceedings or enforcement of a decision “pending an appeal”, is designed to freeze or stop certain consequences of the decision until the appeal is decided: Alberta Energy Regulator v Grant Thornton Limited, 2017 ABCA 278 at paras 58-59. It is not designed to neutralize or reverse the decision itself pending the outcome of the appeal. [16] So, in this case, Mr. Denis may apply to stay a consequence of the finding of contempt, namely the sanction and costs part of the proceeding. However, this Court cannot generally stay an actual decision, such as a finding of contempt. Whether that finding stands or not will be determined in the appeal proper. Clearly, this is what r 14.48(b) contemplates when it refers to “stay proceedings” or “enforcement of a decision”. Even if in some circumstances it might be possible or appropriate to stay a decision, rather than the consequences of the decision, those circumstances do not arise in this case…. The issue also arose in Smit v. Alberta (Director of Saferoads), 2023 ABKB 508, 2023 CarswellAlta 2330. In that case Justice Whitling had made an Order and the Director applied for “a stay of that part of the Decision which allowed the Applicant’s application for judicial review on the ground that the Director had failed or refused to provide the Applicant with a copy of any video or audio recordings of the events at issue, or alternatively to advise her that no such recordings exist.” In deciding that such a stay could not be granted, Justice Whitling referred to Justice Khullar’s decision in Denis v. Sauvageau, supra, and said, at paragraph 3: … The part of the Decision that the Director now seeks to stay does not order the Director or any other party to do anything, and does not direct or allow the continuation of any legal proceedings or enforcement measures. Consequently, there is nothing to stay. This court’s authority “to stay proceedings or enforcement of a decision pending appeal” pursuant to r. 14.48 of the Alberta Rules of Court, AR 124/2010 does not include an authority to suspend the precedential effect of a decision as a matter of stare decisis. … At paragraph 31, his Lordship said: [31] I note that in the above passage from Denis, Khullar J.A. allowed that “it might be possible or appropriate to stay a decision, rather than the consequences of the decision” in some future case. Further, as Smith J.A. noted in Bessette v British Columbia (Attorney General), 2018 BCCA 59 at paras. 20-23, the restrictive approach adopted by Wakeling J.A. in Grant Thornton is arguably contrary to that adopted by Rothstein J. in Baier v Alberta, 2006 SCC 38 at paras. 12-13.[1] But even under the more expansive approach in Baier, an interim order may only be issued to preserve the rights and interests of the parties to the appeal in order to preserve the efficacy of the appellant’s right of appeal. … In Great North Equipment Inc. v. Penney, 2024 ABCA 378, Justice Hawkes said: [7] Single members of this Court, when sitting pursuant to the rules identified above, do not have the ability to grant a stay where the order appealed from granted no affirmative relief. To allow this stay application would be to effectively grant the remedy sought in the full appeal in advance of the appeal. The authorities preclude a stay in such circumstances: Noscenco v Bagayeva, 2015 ABCA 266 at para 7; Denis v Sauvageau, 2022 ABCA 166 at para 15; Dr Vu v College of Physicians & Surgeons of Alberta, 2023 ABCA 377 at paras 14-15, and the authorities cited therein. The rules to which Justice Hawkes referred were Rules 14.37 and 14.48. See also: Banerjee v. Sood, 2024 ABCA 417 at paragraphs 14-18, and Spiess v. Spiess, 2025 ABCA 3 at paragraphs 7-10. 3. Stay of a family law order In A. (D.) v. K. (H.), 2014 ABCA 361, 2014 CarswellAlta 1983, Justice Watson set out the test for granting a stay of a family law order. His Lordship said, at paragraphs 17–21: 17 The test for an application for a stay of a family law order respecting custody and access to children is a modified version of the tripartite test for stays and injunctions pending appeal as set out in the decision of RJR-MacDonald Inc v Canada (Attorney General), [1994] 1 SCR 311: (a) arguable case; (b) irreparable harm and (c) balance of convenience. 18 The modification of the test in that context reflects the fact that, in such cases, the litigation is not a commercial dispute between adults or corporations, and the dominant consideration is the best interests of the children involved: see G(A) v J(J), 2008 ABCA 61 paras 11 to 12, 429 AR 394; MacPhail v Karasek, 2006 ABCA 320 para 3, 397 AR 305; B(C) v C(P), 2003 ABCA 321 para 4, 346 AR 121; S(CL) v S(BR), 2013 ABCA 349 paras 10 to 12, 37 RFL (7th) 112. The character of the modification includes the fact that the realities of such cases tend to blend all three of the criteria, or, put another way, the underlying facts tend to influence all three in a manner which is not the same as in disputes over money. 19 The modifications to the tripartite test, therefore, do not change the essential structure of the test, but they do influence the application of its elements. In the first place, the first step of “arguable case” will likely be met by the existence of credible evidence that the best interests of any child involved have been impacted adversely in a significant manner by the order targeted by the proposed stay, coupled with the existence of an arguable case that the targeted order is flawed in some significant manner and that a stay would mitigate those adverse effects and better serve the best interests of the children: S(CL) v S(BR) at para 12. 20 This is a problematic area for child interests' cases. That is because the child-centric modification thus involved is not intended to destroy finality as itself a key feature in the best interests of children. While such an approach is manifested by notions of deference in appellate law, it is not desirable to subject the trial process to recurring (even tit for tat) efforts by parties to seek fresh opinions by different judges as a case proceeds through the courts. Bastarache J in Van de Perre v Edwards, 2001 SCC 60 paras 11 to 13, [2001] 2 SCR 1014 included this: 13 … First, finality is not merely a social interest; rather, it is particularly important for the parties and children involved in custodial disputes. A child should not be unsure of his or her home for four years, as in this case. Finality is a significant consideration in child custody cases, maybe more so than in support cases, and reinforces deference to the trial judge's decision. Second, an appellate court may only intervene in the decision of a trial judge if he or she erred in law or made a material error in the appreciation of the facts. Custody and access decisions are inherently exercises in discretion. Case-by-case consideration of the unique circumstances of each child is the hallmark of the process. This discretion vested in the trial judge enables a balanced evaluation of the best interests of the child and permits [page1025] courts to respond to the spectrum of factors which can both positively and negatively affect a child. 21 The modification as to the first “arguable case” feature of the test has thus not been converted to a low standard of “any argument will do” merely because the interests of children are involved. Cromwell JA, as he then was in Nova Scotia (Minister of Community Services) v F(B) and W(B), 20013 NSCA 125 para 13, 219 NSR 2d 67 explained that, “there will generally need to be circumstances of a “special and persuasive nature”, usually connected to the risk of harm to the children, in order to persuade the Court to grant a stay”. In G. (S.L.) v. G. (R.T.), 2016 ABCA 186, 2016 CarswellAlta 1119, Madam Justice Schutz said: 21 The well-known test for a stay pending appeal as set out in RJR-MacDonald Inc v Canada (Attorney General), [1994] 1 SCR 311 at 334, 111 DLR (4th) 385 is binding upon this Court. The applicant has the burden of showing that: (i) there is a “serious question to be tried” or, in other words, an arguable issue that is not frivolous and vexatious; (ii) there will be irreparable harm if the stay is not granted; and (iii) the balance of convenience favours granting the stay. 22 The test is modified in a stay application dealing with parenting orders involving children, to reflect the paramount importance of the best interests of the child: B(C) v C(P), 2003 ABCA 321 at para 4, 346 AR 121; F(E) v S(JS) (1995), 174 AR 296 at para 10; MacPhail v Karasek, 2006 ABCA 320 at para 3, 397 AR 305; G(A) v B(J), 2008 ABCA 61 at para 11, 429 AR 394. The test has been described as being modified to require that, in addition to determining whether there is a serious issue to be argued on appeal that is neither frivolous nor vexatious, it is also necessary, in light of the best interests of the child, to consider from that perspective whether the child will suffer irreparable harm resulting from the granting or denial of the stay: Noel v Maj, 2006 ABCA 393 at para 3. See also B(R) v P(D), 2007 PESCAD 19, 269 Nfld & PEIR 190. 23 As was said in CLS v BRS, 2013 ABCA 349 at paras 11–12: It is important to clarify that it is the best interests of the child or children which will have primacy in determining the balance of convenience, not the best interests of the parents. The language in the test as read by the cases makes it clear that it is what the child or children would benefit from, not what the parents might benefit from—not necessarily what the father might like, or what the mother would like, or what their plans may be—that will influence what is in the best interests of the child. Fundamentally the decision as to what the child or children's best interests are, ultimately, is of central importance in relation to an application for a stay. I pause to note that the best interests of the children is a matter which impacts all three parts of the test. To that extent, I agree with the sentiment of Macklin J. in Sopczak v. Gye-Sik, 2011 ABQB 77 at para 10, 95 RFL (6th) 338, where he also observed that “[w] henever courts consider the best interests of the child, there is a serious question to be tried.” … 27 When considering the second and third branches of the test for a stay, irreparable harm and the balance of convenience, the best interests of the child or children will determine the balance of convenience. One has to look at the three parts of the test holistically, connecting irreparable harm with balance of convenience when little children are involved. Those interests will ultimately determine the balance of convenience: CB v PC at para 4, EF v JSS at para 10: AG v JB, 2008 ABCA 61 at paras 11-12, 429 AR 394. It is the “convenience” of the children that matters: EG v Alberta (Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act, Director), 2014 ABCA 237 at para 26. There is a high evidential requirement on the applicant to prove irreparable harm: MacPhail v Karasek, 2006 ABCA 320 at para 3, 397 AR 305. This was the test applied in E.T.T. v. G.T., 2018 ABCA 279, 2018 CarswellAlta 2070. In Jonzon v. Yuill, 2020 ABCA 219, 2020 CarswellAlta 991, 10 Alta. L.R. (7th) 244, Justice Wakeling said (footnotes omitted): [2] The test for a stay of a child-custody or access order consists of three parts. [3] First, has the applicant established that the likelihood the applicant will prevail on the appeal is high enough to justify the conclusion that the appeal is not frivolous or vexatious? The court will not stay an original court's order if the prospects of a successful appeal are very low—hopeless or nearly hopeless. [4] This part of the test is the same whether the stay is sought in the context of a commercial or a family law matter. [5] Most of the time, an appeal court may allow an appeal “only if the original court's decision is the product of a misunderstanding of an important legal principle central to the resolution of the issue, or a factual determination that has no evidentiary basis … or an unfair hearing”. [6] Second, has the applicant established that the child, or the applicant, will suffer irreparable harm if the stay is not granted. “‘Irreparable’ refers to the nature of the harm suffered rather than its magnitude. It is harm which either cannot be quantified in monetary terms or which cannot be cured, usually because one party cannot collect damages from the other”. [7] If the court concludes that the failure to grant a stay will cause the child irreparable harm, assuming that the applicant passes the other two parts of the test, the proper disposition is clear—issue a stay. [8] If the court concludes that a stay will not cause the child irreparable harm, but will cause the applicant irreparable harm, the court should grant a stay, assuming that the applicant passes the other two elements of the test. … [10] The second element of the stay test has been modified to take into account the interests of the child or children. This component does not work this way in commercial stays. [11] Third, has the applicant established that the harm the child or the applicant will suffer if a stay is not granted exceeds the harm the child or the respondent will suffer if a stay is granted? [12] Again, the traditional component has been revised to reflect the fundamental interest in the child's welfare. In FG v. KAV, 2020 ABCA 347, 2020 CarswellAlta 1740, Justice Antonio said: [8] The test for a stay pending appeal is set out in RJR-MacDonald Inc v Canada (Attorney General), 1994 CanLII 117 (SCC), [1994] 1 SCR 311 at 334. The applicant has the burden of showing that i) there is a serious question to be tried, meaning there is an arguable issue that is not frivolous and vexatious; ii) there will be irreparable harm if the stay is not granted; and iii) the balance of convenience favours granting the stay. [9] The three-part test is modified when dealing with a stay application involving a child, to reflect the paramount importance of the best interests of the child: CB v PC, 2003 ABCA 321 at para 4; CLS v BRS, 2013 ABCA 349 at paras 10–12; Bourgeois v Caldwell, 2017 ABCA 328 at para 7. Analysis i)—Serious question [10] The threshold of whether there is a serious question to be tried is low. The analysis does not require a detailed assessment of the merits of the case: CB v PC, supra at para 3. Courts recognize that that there is often a serious question to be tried when the best interests of children are involved: CLS v BRS, supra at para 12, citing Sopczak v Gye-Sik, 2011 ABQB 77 at para 10; Bourgeois v Caldwell, supra at para 9. However, just because the best interests of children are involved does not mean that “any argument will do”: DA v HK, 2014 ABCA 361 at para 21; Baker v Hunter, 2015 ABCA 309 at para 10. An “arguable case” will likely be made out where there is credible evidence that the best interests of the child have been impacted adversely in a significant manner by the lower court's order, coupled an arguable case that the targeted order is flawed in some significant manner and that a stay would mitigate those adverse effects and better serve the best interests of the children: DA v HK, supra at para 19. Due to the fact-based and discretionary nature of family law cases, and the desire to promote finality in family law litigation, considerable deference is given to a trial judge's findings: Hickey v Hickey, 1999 CanLII 691 (SCC), [1999] 2 SCR 518 at para 10; Spencer v Spencer, 2005 ABCA 262 at para 2. … ii)—Irreparable harm and balance of convenience [13] In Baker v Hunter, supra at para 11, the Court summarized the approach to the second and third parts of the modified test for a stay pending appeal as follows: The modified second and third parts of the test mandate a consideration of whether the children will suffer irreparable harm from the denial of a stay, and it is those interests that will ultimately determine the balance of convenience. These parts of the test must be considered holistically, as irreparable harm is intricately connected with the balance of convenience when children are involved: AG v JB, 2008 ABCA 61 at para 12, 429 AR 394. [14] Irreparable harm to the best interests of a child is not found in a mere disruption to a child's life: Noel v Maj, 2006 ABCA 393 at para 8; MacPhail v Karasek, 2006 ABCA 320 at paras 6–8; GR v CM, 2003 ABCA 268 at paras 17, 19. There must be evidence of special circumstances that demonstrate potential harm to the child, or some harm that is “real and significant” and is more than a transitory disturbance: MacPhail v Karasek, supra at para 6; DA v HK, supra at para 29. [15] Any harm to the parents from the denial of a stay is subordinate to the best interests of the children: ibid. Further, the only convenience that will really matter is the convenience of the children: EG v Alberta (Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act, Director), 2014 ABCA 237 at para 26. In AF v. DS, 2021 ABCA 136, 2021 CarswellAlta 905, Justice Feehan gave this helpful summary: [6] The well-known tripartite test for a stay pending appeal is set out in RJR-MacDonald Inc v Canada (Attorney General), 1994 CanLII 117 (SCC), [1994] 1 SCR 311, 334, 111 DLR (4th) 385. The applicant has the burden of showing that: (i) there is a serious question to be tried, an arguable issue that is not frivolous or vexatious; (ii) there will be irreparable harm if the stay is not granted; and (iii) the balance of convenience favours granting the stay. [7] The test to be applied in matters involving parenting is the tripartite test, modified to reflect the paramount importance of the best interests of the child: CB v PC, 2003 ABCA 321, para 4, 24 Alta LR (4th) 53; AR v JU, 2020 ABCA 337, para 6. The test is modified to consider, in light of the best interests of the child, if the child will suffer irreparable harm resulting from the granting or denial of the stay: AR, para 6; Noel v Maj, 2006 ABCA 393, para 3. The best interest of the child is not necessarily the best interest of the parents, or what the parents may like, or dependant on what their plans may be: CLS v BRS, 2013 ABCA 349, para 11. Irreparable harm to the best interests of a child is not found in mere disruption to the children's lives. There must be evidence of special circumstances that demonstrate potential harm to the child, or some harm that is “real and significant” and is more than a transitory disturbance: Lloyd-Martinez v Martinez, 2021 ABCA 13, para 15. 4. Generally In LDS v. SCA, 2019 ABCA 312, 2019 CarswellAlta 1799, Justice Feehan said: [13] A stay pending appeal can only stay that which has been appealed. … … [14] The test for a stay pending appeal is the same as for the grant of an interlocutory injunction: Manitoba (Attorney General) v Metropolitan Stores (MTS) Ltd, 1987 CanLII 79 (SCC), [1987] 1 SCR 110, p 127, 38 DLR (4th) 321; RJR-MacDonald Inc v Canada (Attorney General), 1994 CanLII 117 (SCC), [1994] 1 SCR 311, p 334, 111 DLR (4th) 385. [15] In RJR-MacDonald, the Supreme Court of Canada set out a tripartite test: 1. There must be a serious question to be tried; 2. The applicant must suffer irreparable harm if the application is refused; and 3. On a balance of convenience it must be determined which party would suffer greater harm from the granting or refusal of the remedy (RJR-MacDonald, p 334). [16] The first branch of the test is satisfied if the court can find that “the claim is not frivolous or vexatious.” The threshold is a low one: “[t]he judge on the application must make a preliminary assessment of the merits” and be satisfied that the application is neither vexatious nor frivolous (RJR-MacDonald, pp 337 and 348); see also: Santoro v Bank of Montreal, 2018 ABCA 264 (CanLII), para 4. This test is to be determined by a motions judge on the basis of common sense (RJR-MacDonald, 348). Two exceptions apply to the general rule that a judge should not engage in an extensive review of the merits: when the result of the interlocutory motion will in effect amount to a final determination of the action (pp 338 and 348) and when the question presents itself as a simple question of law alone (pp 339 and 348). [17] It is worth noting this first branch of the tripartite test is modified for the grant of a mandatory injunction to the test originally set out in American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd, [1975] AC 396; the applicant must show a strong prima facie case: R v Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, 2018 SCC 5 (CanLII), paras 15–18, [2018] 1 SCR 196; Modry v Alberta Health Services, 2015 ABCA 265 (CanLII), paras 36-37, 388 DLR (4th) 352; ServiceMaster of Canada Limited v Meyer, 2019 ABCA 130 (CanLII), para 105; Alan Arsenault Holdings Ltd v TDL Group Corp, 2016 ABQB 97 (CanLII), para 28. [18] The test however on a stay application of a mandatory injunction is the former: a serious question to be tried. This is because the results of a stay application, whether granted or refused, do not require any party to take a positive course of action: Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, para 16. [19] In the second branch of the test the issue to be decided is “whether a refusal to grant relief could so adversely affect the applicants' own interests that the harm could not be remedied if the eventual decision on the merits does not accord with the result of the interlocutory application” (RJR-MacDonald, p 341). Irreparable harm refers to the nature of the harm suffered rather than its magnitude: “[i]t is harm which either cannot be quantified in monetary terms or which cannot be cured” (pp 341 and 348). In some cases, inability to recover costs in conjunction with other factors qualifies as irreparable harm: Canadian Natural Resources Ltd v Wood Buffalo (Regional Municipality), 2011 ABQB 220 (CanLII), paras 62–69, 516 AR 51, and where an appeal is rendered moot without the granting of a stay there is a rebuttable presumption that irreparable harm is inevitable: Patel v Tulan, 2015 ABCA 384 (CanLII), paras 16-17, 612 AR 42. [20] In the third branch of the test, balance of convenience, consideration must be had of the public interest, both the concerns of society generally and the particular interests of identifiable groups, as well as the damage that may accrue to the parties (RJR-MacDonald, pp 343 and 348). The public interest considerations weigh more heavily in a suspension case than in an exemption case. In Triple Five Corp. v. United Western Communications Ltd. (1994), 19 Alta. L.R. (3d) 153 (C.A.), Kerans J.A. considered an application for a stay of the vacation of an injunction. In considering the test to be applied, he said the following (at p. 155): Counsel all agree that the authorities indicate that, on an application for a stay, the same authorities generally govern as those that govern an application for an interim injunction. That approach might work in most cases, but the difficulty in this case is that it in effect puts me in a position of either rehearing the interim injunction application or sitting on an appeal of it, neither of which is satisfactory. The Court of Appeal Act says that a quorum of this court for the purposes of hearing and deciding an appeal is three judges and that one judge can only hear and decide matters incidental to an appeal. Therefore, in my view, I do not have authority today to make a decision that is tantamount to hearing and deciding an appeal. This conundrum has always made applications for stays difficult for me. Where it can be shown that the relief sought would be nugatory if a stay was not allowed and there is no harm to the respondent, I have always granted a stay unless I could say that there was no reasonable possibility of success on the appeal. On the other hand, it is often the case that the granting of a stay pending the hearing of an appeal, with all the attendant delays, would render nugatory the rights of the respondent invoked to get the order under appeal. That is exactly this case… The only answer, it seems to me is to get some more judges in here and hear this appeal as quickly as possible… With respect to the test to be applied in an application for a stay, the Supreme Court of Canada said: Generally, the same principles should be applied by a court whether the remedy sought is an injunction or a stay. In [Manitoba (Attorney General) v. Metropolitan Stores (M.T.S.) Ltd., [1987] 1 S.C.R. 110], at p. 127, Beetz J. expressed the position in these words: A stay of proceedings and an interlocutory injunction are remedies of the same nature. In the absence of a different test prescribed by statute, they have sufficient characteristics in common to be governed by the same rules and the courts have rightly tended to apply to the granting of interlocutory stay the principles which they follow with respect to interlocutory injunctions. … Metropolitan Stores adopted a three-stage test for courts to apply when considering an application for either a stay or an interlocutory injunction. First, a preliminary assessment must be made of the merits of the case to ensure that there is a serious question to be tried. Secondly, it must be determined whether the applicant would suffer irreparable harm if the application were refused. Finally, an assessment must be made as to which of the parties would suffer greater harm from the granting or refusal of the remedy pending a decision on the merits … Prior to the decision of the House of Lords in American Cyanamid Co. v. Ethicon Ltd., [1975] A.C. 396, an applicant for interlocutory relief was required to demonstrate a “strong prima facie case” on the merits in order to satisfy the first test. In American Cyanamid, however, Lord Diplock stated that an applicant need no longer demonstrate a strong prima facie case. Rather, it would suffice if he or she could satisfy the court that “the claim is not frivolous or vexatious; in other words, that there is a serious question to be tried”. The American Cyanamid standard is now generally accepted by the Canadian courts, subject to the occasional reversion to a stricter standard: see Robert J. Sharpe, Injunctions and Specific Performance (2nd ed. 1992), at pp. 2-13 to 2-20… What then are the indicators of “a serious question to be tried”? There are no specific requirements which must be met in order to satisfy this test. The threshold is a low one. The judge on the application must make a preliminary assessment of the merits of the case … Once satisfied that the application is neither vexatious nor frivolous, the motions judge should proceed to consider the second and third tests, even if of the opinion that the plaintiff is unlikely to succeed at trial. A prolonged examination of the merits is generally neither necessary nor desirable. Two exceptions apply to the general rule that a judge should not engage in an extensive review of the merits. The first arises when the result of the interlocutory motion will in effect amount to a final determination of the action. This will be the case either when the right which the applicant seeks to protect can only be exercised immediately or not at all, or when the result of the application will impose such hardship on one party as to remove any potential benefit from proceeding to trial … Beetz J. determined in Metropolitan Stores, at p. 128, that “[t]he second test consists in deciding whether the litigant who seeks the interlocutory injunction would, unless the injunction is granted, suffer irreparable harm”. The harm which might be suffered by the respondent, should the relief sought be granted, has been considered by some courts at this stage. We are of the opinion that this is more appropriately dealt with in the third part of the analysis. Any alleged harm to the public interest should also be considered at that stage. At this stage the only issue to be decided is whether a refusal to grant relief could so adversely affect the applicants' own interests that the harm could not be remedied if the eventual decision on the merits does not accord with the result of the interlocutory application. “Irreparable” refers to the nature of the harm suffered rather than its magnitude. The present case raises the subtle point of where in the tripartite test the public interest is to be weighed. [7] The Director argues that the public interest must be considered at both the second and third stages of the tripartite test. Thomson, and its approach to irreparable harm, has since gained traction in SafeRoads stay applications. At para 12, the Court held: “Where a government authority is involved, the public interest is a special factor forming part of the consideration at both the second and third stages of the test: RJR MacDonald Inc.” The Director submits that this is a correct statement of the law that binds the Court. [9] This statement of the tripartite test in Thomson was followed in Tarnow v Alberta (Director of SafeRoads), 2021 ABQB 602 at para 25. Thomson has also been applied on two occasions by the Alberta Transportation Safety Board: Re Autoguard Inspection Services Ltd., 2019 ABTSB 1472 at para 17; and Re 1790445 Alberta Ltd., 2020 ABTSB 1913 at para 10. The same articulation of where the public interest is to be considered in the tripartite test, though without reference to Thomson, is also found in Trca v Alberta (Director of SafeRoads), 2022 ABQB 85 at para 9 and Tunke v Alberta (Director of SafeRoads), 2022 ABQB 531 at para 12. [10] Thomson, though a decision of the Court of Appeal, should not be followed with respect to the content of the second stage of the tripartite test as it is incorrect in holding that public interest is to be considered when assessing the irreparable harm to an applicant that does not assert the public interest. Though the circumstances of this case do not fit within the limited exceptions to the principle of vertical stare decisis set out in Canada (Attorney General) v Bedford, 2013 SCC 72 at para 42, there are nevertheless three good reasons to depart from precedent: (1) the decision is inconsistent with first principles and the leading Supreme Court of Canada authority, RJR; (2) the Court of Appeal in later decisions follows the approach that flows from first principles and a correct reading of RJR; and (3) in a later decision the same Justice states the law correctly, suggesting that the earlier statement in Thomson was a slip or a transcription error. …. [12] On an injunction or stay application, the applicant's burden is to demonstrate on a balance of probabilities that an injunction or stay should issue. Paperny JA, writing for the majority in AC and JF at para 55 observed that “[t]he harm engendered by the failure to grant interlocutory relief is generally assessed from the standpoint of the person seeking to benefit from that interlocutory relief.” Justice Sharpe, writing extra-judicially, explained that to satisfy the second stage of the tripartite test, an applicant “must show an immediate risk of harm that will occur before the case reaches trial and that cannot be compensated or remedied other than through the granting of an interlocutory injunction”: Injunctions & Specific Performance at § 2:7. [13] At the second stage of the tripartite test, the focus is only on the apprehended harm to the applicant not on countervailing interests. RJR at 338 makes it clear that, at this stage, “the applicant must convince the court that it will suffer irreparable harm.” The public interest is only considered at the second stage of the tripartite test where an applicant – typically, government or a governmental authority – claims to represent the public interest. Where the applicant does not claim to represent the public interest, the third stage of the tripartite test – the balance of convenience – is where the public interest asserted by a respondent is weighed: AC and JF at para 32. [14] The error in Thomson flows from a misreading of RJR. … … [16] Rothstein JA, as he then was, in Sawridge Band v Canada, 2004 FCA 16 summarized the law concerning where in the tripartite test the public interest is to be weighed that emerged from RJR. He wrote at para 48: “Ordinarily, the public interest is considered only in the third branch of the test. However, where, as here, the government is the applicant in a motion for interlocutory relief, the public interest must also be considered in the second stage.” [17] Thomson and the cases that follow it or use the same formulation of the tripartite test stating that the public interest should be considered at the second stage of the tripartite test even though the government authority claiming to represent the public interest was the respondent are anomalous. … [18] There is nothing in Thomson to suggest that Wittmann JA intended to change the law stated in RJR; indeed, his intention appears to be to provide a recitation of the tripartite as set out in RJR. Even Wittmann JA, it seems, did not consider his statement in Thomson as to where the public interest was to be considered in the tripartite test to be noteworthy. Five years later, without reference to Thomson, Wittmann ACJ (as he was by that time) explained how the public interest is to be considered in the tripartite test in Morrow v Zhang, 2008 ABQB 125 at para 13 in terms similar to that of Rothstein JA in Sawridge: “where the government is the party making the application for a stay, the issue of public interest will be considered as an aspect of irreparable harm at the second stage as well as at the third stage” [emphasis added]. Wittmann ACJ's statement of the law in Morrow suggests that his earlier statement of the law in Thomson was a slip or perhaps incorrectly transcribed. [19] Considering the public interest asserted by a respondent only at the third stage of the tripartite test promotes analytical clarity. Limiting consideration of the public interest to the weighing of the balance of convenience does not diminish the importance of the public interest or mean that it weighs any less in the overall analysis. Indeed, maintaining a conceptually coherent approach to the tripartite test brings the interests being balanced at the third stage into sharper relief. 5. Exceptional circumstances In Santoro v. In the circumstances of this case, one must consider the meaning of the word “impractical” and the issue of onus. Onus Absent guidance in a specific rule or statute, the general rule of procedure is that the person who asserts must prove. To succeed here, Burgoin, who is asserting, must show that an application to the judge appealed from was practical. In my view, he has not. No evidence was led as to why the application for a stay was brought before Chrumka, J., rather than Moshansky, J. I note, however, that Moshansky, J., was a duty judge during the week of July 3, 2001. The duty roster discloses that during the week of July 23, Chrumka, J., was a duty judge. Other than this factual context, there is no evidence before me suggesting that it was practical for Moshansky, J., to hear the stay application. On the question of onus, in my view, Burgoin has failed to satisfy me that it was practical for Moshansky, J., to hear the application and therefore his challenge to my jurisdiction must fail. In this regard, I have considered the meaning of the word “impractical” in Rule 508. Many cases distinguish between the words “practical” or “impractical” and “practicable” or “impracticable”. Some do not. Where distinction is made, it has been said that “practicable” has to do with something which is capable of being done, whereas “practical” denotes whether it can be done usefully or not at too great a cost: United Services Funds (Trustee of) v. Ontario (Ministry of Labour) (1991), 9 C.O.H.S.C. 91 at 96 (Ont. Adjud.) Novick (Vice Adjudicator) stated that there is a distinction between “impracticable” and “impractical”, the latter being a word which connotes a lower standard. Thus, to bring oneself under Rule 503(3) (sic) [the reference should be to Rule 508(3)] where a different judge than from the one appealed from has entertained the stay application, and the stay application is attempted de novo before this court, if making the application to the judge appealed from was “impractical”, this court has de novo jurisdiction conferred upon it by Rule 508(3). The onus of a party challenging that jurisdiction is to satisfy this court on that application that making the application for a stay to the judge appealed from was practical, or at least to lead some evidence that it was practical. Interlocutory Orders Made in Trials The unusual aspect of this appeal is not that it is from an interlocutory order, but an interlocutory order made in the course of a trial. Unlike other jurisdictions, Alberta by R. 508 permits an appeal, without leave, from an interlocutory order of a judge of the Court of Queen's Bench. In jurisdictions where leave to appeal an interlocutory order must be obtained, the rule seems to be that leave is almost always denied where the order is made in the course of a trial. A question arises about Alberta practice. Appeals of this sort in civil cases are extremely rare, indeed one might say almost non-existent, at least in the recent past. Novelty, of course, is no reason to refuse to hear an appeal. The need to protect the due administration of justice, however, is such a reason. This court can and should refuse to exercise its admitted jurisdiction to hear an appeal when to do so would suffer every trial to be delayed while each decision made by the judge in the course of a trial is the subject of a separate review. In general, a party who feels aggrieved must await the final verdict. Only then should this court review for possible error. In our view, this system historically has proven to offer an adequate remedy for almost any injustice that might arise during the course of a trial. In our view, the only exception to the general rule should be where the appellant can show that later review will not produce a just result. Alberta Tank Ltd. v. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (1987), 53 Alta. L.R. (2d) 190 at 191-92 (C.A.). And in another decision the Court of Appeal also said: We are all of the view that this court can refuse to hear an appeal when to do so is to abuse the judicial process. The disruption to the trial process caused by appeals from interlocutory orders made in the middle of a trial is obvious and, except perhaps for the most unusual circumstance, this disruption is an abuse of process. Any other rule would permit trials never to be finished. Cascade Development Corp. v. B.S.C. Pension Fund Trustee Ltd. (1988), 63 Alta. L.R. (2d) 394 at 395 (C.A.). In Deloitte Haskins & Sells v. Coopers & Lybrand Inc. (1996), 37 Alta. L.R. (3d) 64 (C.A.), Madam Justice Russell, at pp. 68–71, analyzed a stay application (in respect of an interlocutory order) in the following manner: While the prima facie test no longer needs to be proven in private law matters, absent complexities similar to Charter issues, a preliminary assessment of the applicant's success on the appeal must be considered. Since this is an interlocutory matter, the burden on the applicant is not as great as it would be if the matter had been finally disposed of at trial. The ultimate rights of the parties will not be finally determined as a result of this application. If the stay is not granted, the applicant may still proceed with its third party action, and may yet successfully defend the plaintiff's claim. However, what the application must show is a potential for success both on the appeal and in the ultimate result. The stronger the potential, the greater the likelihood that a stay will be granted, subject to a consideration of the other two factors … Harm is irreparable if it cannot be adequately compensated in damages. “Irreparable” refers to the nature of the harm, and not its magnitude: [RJR-Macdonald v. Canada (Attorney General), [1994] 1 S.C.R. 311 at p. 341]… On the side of the applicant it is said that inconvenience to the plaintiff investors is minimal because the money is not at risk, although there will be a further delay in distribution. The greater risk is that the applicant will be deprived of some right of recovery if the plaintiffs' action succeeds … On the side of the respondent it is said the inconvenience to the investment contract holders is substantial. Many are elderly, and some are dependent upon these investments. Some have died since the proceedings began, and the longer the distribution is delayed the greater the risk that more will be deprived of the enjoyment of these monies in their lifetime. The prospect of individual hardship overshadows corporate loss. I am reminded however, that financial hardship arising from a stay would be transient. A stay would not foreclose substantive rights; the denial of a stay would … Considering the fact that the monies are not at risk if the stay is granted, and the possibility of an expedited appeal with terms that would mitigate prejudice to the plaintiffs, I find the greater harm would be suffered by the applicant if the stay is not granted. 11. Rule 14.48 Not Confined to Appeals from Queen's Bench In addition, it is perfectly clear under the Judicature Act and the Court of Appeal Act that the Court of Appeal still has all the general powers which the old Supreme Court of Alberta had. The Court of Appeal Act specifically enables the Lieutenant-Governor-in-Council to make rules governing the practice and procedure of the court, and the Alberta Rules of Court were made under that power. I cannot see anything in the portion of the Alberta Rules of Court dealing with appeals to the Court of Appeal which restricts all those Rules to appeals from the Court of Queen's Bench. In particular, I cannot see anything which confines rule 508 to appeals from the Court of Queen's Bench. Therefore it is my conclusion that under rule 508 I can consider the question of a stay of execution of a Development Appeal Board order appealed from. Armstrong v. Athabasca No.1 (County) (1990), 120 A.R. 285 at 286 (C.A.). 12. Rule Only Applies to Appeals to Court of Appeal In Bourque v. Tensfeldt, 2017 ABCA 236, 2017 CarswellAlta 1758, the Applicant sought an order staying enforcement of an order for costs made by a Master. Justice Greckol dismissed the application on the basis that the Court of Appeal did not have jurisdiction to stay an order which was not being appealed to the Court of Appeal. Her Ladyship said at paragraphs 5–6: 5 There is a preliminary issue regarding this Court's jurisdiction to stay enforcement of the Master's costs order of $5,500. The costs order has not been appealed to this Court and, indeed, cannot be: r 14.4(4) of the Alberta Rules of Court, AR 124/2010, vol 1 [Rules]. The costs decision of the Master may be directly appealed to a justice of the Court of Queen's Bench: r 6.14(1). 6 Since Ms. Bourque has not appealed, and cannot appeal, the Master's costs order to this Court, a single judge of this Court has no jurisdiction to stay its enforcement. This Court only has the jurisdiction to stay enforcement of a decision pending appeal of that decision to this Court: r 14.48. Accordingly, Ms. Bourque's application for a stay of that order is dismissed. 13. Failure to Prosecute Appeal To get a stay fully intending to prosecute the appeal diligently, and then to fail to prosecute it would be bad enough … To get a stay not intending to prosecute the appeal diligently seems to me an abuse of process. See Mireau v. Saskatchewan (Minister of Justice), [1995] 4 W.W.R. 389 (Sask. C.A.). The English Court of Appeal says that counsel cannot ethically take instructions to file an appeal and then do nothing with it without telling that to the Court: Grosvenor (Mayfair) Estates v. Raja, The Times, 2 Nov. 1990. I can see some possible exceptions to that statement, such as a few weeks to get proper instructions. But as a general principle, I agree with the English Court of Appeal … There are resemblances between an interlocutory injunction and a stay of execution pending appeal, and so much the same criteria apply to both: Metropolitan Stores (MTS) Ltd. v. Manitoba Commercial Workers, Local 832, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 110 …RJR-MacDonald Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General), [1994] 1 S.C.R. 311 …Frost v. Assn. of Architects (Alberta) (1995), 30 Alta. L.R. (3d) 93 (C.A.), at 96, per Côté J.A. Mr. Justice Côté referred to the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal decision in Mireau v. Saskatchewan (Minister of Justice), [1995] 4 W.W.R. 389. In that case, the Saskatchewan court said at p. 391: When counsel goes on record for an appellant he thereby incurs an obligation to keep the matter moving by complying with the rules respecting the requisition of a transcript of the evidence (where applicable) but also any directions that the Court may make… This responsibility exists in both criminal and civil proceedings. We adopt the reasons of Côté J.A. in R. v. Van Le (November 25, 1994) (Alta. C.A. (Chambers)) (unreported) [now reported R. v. Le (1994), 162 A.R. 4], in the following passages: I must point out that when counsel goes on the record for the appellant on a criminal appeal and gets bail for his client, he thereby incurs some very serious obligations to keep the matter moving. Those obligations cannot be delegated, and if he wants to get out of them, he should apply to be relieved of them, or to have them extended, or to have himself taken off the record as counsel. This is not the first time when the Court has seen an appeal move too slowly, though the appellant is on bail, when there has been a change of counsel. That can not only slow things down, but leave the Court faced with a lawyer who is not the one who gave any undertakings or got the bail, in the absence of the lawyer who incurred those obligations and is ‘no longer acting’ in the matter. This is not a correct understanding of the duties of counsel. Unless and until the Court takes the obligations off the shoulders of the counsel who first incurred them, they remain on his shoulders. If a second counsel comes along, that may add a second person with a duty, but it does not automatically remove the duty of the first one. … In circumstances where an appellant decides to take no further steps counsel should obtain instructions to immediately abandon the appeal, thereby saving unnecessary applications and consequent costs. In Union Tractor Ltd. v. Horseshoe Contracting Ltd. (2002), 1 Alta. L.R. (4th) 33 (C.A.), Côté J.A., said, at pp. 35–36: An appellant who gets a stay of execution has an obligation to prosecute his appeal promptly and diligently. That does not mean merely adhering to deadlines in the Rules. … It means taking each step so soon as is reasonably possible with due diligence. It is no excuse that the appellant's counsel is a busy sole practitioner; Alberta is not short of lawyers. … There is nothing novel or obscure about that rule of law. … It is the practice of the Alberta Court of Appeal to grant stays of execution pending appeal only upon strict terms. … If there is no express term of the stay order, that duty of prompt prosecution is nevertheless implied. If the appeal dawdles, the stay may be ended. 14. Appeal from a Denial of Stay In G. (S.) v. Alberta (Family & Social Services) (1999), (sub nom. S.G. v. Alberta (Minister of Family & Social Services)) 237 A.R. 378 (C.A.), a single judge of the Court of Appeal had denied an application for a stay of proceedings pending appeal. The appellant sought to have that denial reviewed by a three judge panel of the court. At p. 380, the court said: We know of no provision for appeal to a panel of three judges from denial by a single judge of a stay of execution of judgment… We listened to S.G. only because his materials contained serious allegations of wrongdoing. In no circumstances should this be interpreted to mean that this or a similar procedure to review the decision of a single justice of appeal acting under rule 508 has been approved by us. 15. Setting Aside a Stay Order In Dornan v. Dornan Estate (2002), 98 Alta. L.R. (3d) 29 (C.A.), (2007) 409 A.R. 83 (Alta. C.A. [In Chambers]) at p. 85. Russell J.A. then considered the question of who bore the onus on the application to set aside the stay. She held that the onus fell on the party seeking to continue the stay. At p. 33, she said: In Queen's Bench, the respondents sought a stay of the sale order. Accordingly they bore the onus of establishing that the tripartite test for a stay was met. In this court, it is the applicants who have applied for relief. Ordinarily, the general rule that he who asserts must prove would suggest that the applicants bear the onus of proof before this court. However, an application to this court under rule 508(3), subsequent to an application for a stay to Queen's Bench, is an application de novo. Hence, this court must consider the matter afresh, as if it were being considered for the first time. The onus is on the party seeking the imposition or continued imposition of the stay. In Lausen v. Alberta (Director of SafeRoads), 2022 ABCA 313, 2022 CarswellAlta 2489, Justice Ho gave this summary of the test to be applied on an application to set aside a stay (with an added comment on what to do when the stay order sought to be set aside was granted on consent of the parties): [12] On an application to set aside a stay, the court must consider the well-known tripartite test set out in RJR-MacDonald Inc v Canada (Attorney General), 1994 CanLII 117 (SCC), [1994] 1 SCR 311, 111 DLR (4th) 385, but courts may also address additional factors, including delay, inequitable conduct, and policy considerations: Dreco Energy Services Ltd v Wenzel, 2008 ABCA 290 at para 27. [13] A stay may be varied or set aside where there has been a change in circumstances, since it was granted, that would lead to a different assessment of one or more of the elements of the tripartite test: see Patel v Alberta (Securities Commission), 2019 ABCA 13 at para 11. The circumstances of this application are, however, unique in that this stay order was entered into on consent and there is no record from the court below considering the tripartite test. Regardless, I am able to consider factors such as delay and policy considerations which, in my view, are determinative of this application.
