Reg.
Test for a stay In Knelsen Sand & Gravel Ltd. v.
Harco Enterprises Ltd., 2021 ABCA 362, 2021 CarswellAlta 2716, Justice Wakeling gave this very helpful summary of the law (footnotes omitted): [38] The standard stay test has three components.
[39] First, does the applicant's claim present a serious issue to be tried, or is it frivolous, vexatious, baseless, hopeless, not arguable or has extremely low prospects of success?
[40] Second, would the applicant suffer irreparable harm if relief is not granted, or could a subsequent remedy, such as a damages order, adequately compensate the applicant?
[41] Third, would the applicant suffer greater harm than the respondent if relief were denied, or would the harm to the respondent from granting the application exceed it?
[42] A court must consider the consequences of granting or refusing a stay of execution of a judgment and ascertain whose interests should be put at risk.
An applicant may allege that it needs the funds to prosecute an appeal or that it is unlikely the respondent will repay to the applicant a sum paid under a judgment subsequently reversed on appeal.

The respondent, on the other hand, may claim that the passage of time associated with a stay may reduce to an unacceptable degree the likelihood it will be able to enforce its judgment if the applicant's appeal is dismissed.

Or the respondent may assert, like the applicant, that it needs the money to retain counsel to defend the judgement under appeal. “[T]he essential question is whether there is a risk of injustice to one or other or both parties if it grants or refuses a stay.” [43] An applicant who satisfies all three components is entitled to its relief unless the “applicant has not applied promptly for relief or other deficiencies equity traditionally recognized exist”.
An applicant who fails to pass any one component is not entitled to relief.
[44] Irreparable harm is typically viewed as harm that cannot be quantified in monetary terms.
But back in 1994 Justices Sopinka and Cory opined that it can also be harm that cannot be cured because the applicant could not collect money from the respondent.
The irreparable harm inquiry must reflect the context—the applicant seeks relief from having to pay a money judgment.
[45] Most of the time a judgment debtor will stumble at this hurdle.

A judgment-debtor applicant who pays a judgment creditor before a successful appeal occurs generally still has a viable and adequate remedy—sue the judgment creditor for the return of the money paid under a judgment that has been vacated or ask the appeal court reversing the judgment to order the respondent to repay the money unjustly received.

[46] But circumstances may exist where having to pay out a money judgment can cause the applicant irreparable harm—for example, if the applicant would be unable to recover those amounts should it be successful on appeal, or if making the payment would cause the applicant harm that could not be monetarily quantified, such as putting it out of business.

[47] An applicant who can demonstrate that there is a reasonable prospect the respondent will not be able to repay the judgment following a successful appeal if a stay is not granted, provided the respondent cannot establish that it has both the ability and intention to repay it, has made out irreparable harm.
[48] The court may vitiate the harm arising from concerns about payment by ordering a party to give an undertaking and post security into court as a condition of either granting or refusing the stay.
[49] This is somewhat similar to the undertakings required of an applicant upon obtaining an interlocutory injunction.
Undertakings as to damages arising from a stay do not appear to be usual notwithstanding that, in effect, a stay of execution and injunction may well share similar features.
In Venini v.

Venini, 2023 ABKB 601, Justice Marion gave this summary of the applicable principles: [8] The test for determining whether the appeal is arguable or not has a low threshold….It does not require an examination of the merits of the case, but rather simply involves an assessment of whether the appeal is frivolous or vexatious…. ….
[13] …irreparable harm usually must be that of the applicant and not potential harm to third parties or entities without legal standing…. ….
[15] Further, evidence of irreparable harm must be clear and not speculative…. ….
C.
Does the Balance of Convenience Support a Stay?

[28] At this stage, the court must consider which of the parties will suffer greater harm from the granting or refusal of the stay pending the appeal….The court must assess the severity of the harm and identify the party that should not be ordered to endure that adversity associated with either granting or dismissing the application because it exceeds that [which] the other party will experience….
Effect of a stay In Denis v.
Sauvageau, 2022 ABCA 166, 2022 CarswellAlta 1158, Khullar, J.A. discussed the effect of a stay of proceedings.
What is being stayed?

Her Ladyship said: [13] The application is brought under r 14.48(b) of the Rules of Court which provides that “[a] n application to stay proceedings or enforcement of a decision pending appeal may be made … to a single appeal judge …” (emphasis added).
[14] A preliminary issue is that it appears that Mr.
Denis is asking this Court to stay two different things.
First, he asks the Court to stay the finding of contempt pending his appeal.
Second, he wants to stay the proceedings so that the trial court will not address sanction or costs while he appeals the finding of contempt.

[15] A stay of proceedings or enforcement of a decision “pending an appeal”, is designed to freeze or stop certain consequences of the decision until the appeal is decided: Alberta Energy Regulator v Grant Thornton Limited, 2017 ABCA 278 at paras 58-59.
It is not designed to neutralize or reverse the decision itself pending the outcome of the appeal.
[16] So, in this case, Mr.
Denis may apply to stay a consequence of the finding of contempt, namely the sanction and costs part of the proceeding.
However, this Court cannot generally stay an actual decision, such as a finding of contempt.
Whether that finding stands or not will be determined in the appeal proper.
Clearly, this is what r 14.48(b) contemplates when it refers to “stay proceedings” or “enforcement of a decision”.
Even if in some circumstances it might be possible or appropriate to stay a decision, rather than the consequences of the decision, those circumstances do not arise in this case….
The issue also arose in Smit v.
Alberta (Director of Saferoads), 2023 ABKB 508, 2023 CarswellAlta 2330.

In that case Justice Whitling had made an Order and the Director applied for “a stay of that part of the Decision which allowed the Applicant’s application for judicial review on the ground that the Director had failed or refused to provide the Applicant with a copy of any video or audio recordings of the events at issue, or alternatively to advise her that no such recordings exist.” In deciding that such a stay could not be granted, Justice Whitling referred to Justice Khullar’s decision in Denis v.

Sauvageau, supra, and said, at paragraph 3: … The part of the Decision that the Director now seeks to stay does not order the Director or any other party to do anything, and does not direct or allow the continuation of any legal proceedings or enforcement measures.
Consequently, there is nothing to stay.
This court’s authority “to stay proceedings or enforcement of a decision pending appeal” pursuant to r.

14.48 of the Alberta Rules of Court, AR 124/2010 does not include an authority to suspend the precedential effect of a decision as a matter of stare decisis. … At paragraph 31, his Lordship said: [31] I note that in the above passage from Denis, Khullar J.A. allowed that “it might be possible or appropriate to stay a decision, rather than the consequences of the decision” in some future case.
Further, as Smith J.A. noted in Bessette v British Columbia (Attorney General), 2018 BCCA 59 at paras.
20-23, the restrictive approach adopted by Wakeling J.A. in Grant Thornton is arguably contrary to that adopted by Rothstein J. in Baier v Alberta, 2006 SCC 38 at paras.

12-13.[1] But even under the more expansive approach in Baier, an interim order may only be issued to preserve the rights and interests of the parties to the appeal in order to preserve the efficacy of the appellant’s right of appeal. … In Great North Equipment Inc. v.

Penney, 2024 ABCA 378, Justice Hawkes said: [7] Single members of this Court, when sitting pursuant to the rules identified above, do not have the ability to grant a stay where the order appealed from granted no affirmative relief.
To allow this stay application would be to effectively grant the remedy sought in the full appeal in advance of the appeal.
The authorities preclude a stay in such circumstances: Noscenco v Bagayeva, 2015 ABCA 266 at para 7
Denis v Sauvageau, 2022 ABCA 166 at para 15
Dr Vu v College of Physicians & Surgeons of Alberta, 2023 ABCA 377 at paras 14-15, and the authorities cited therein.
The rules to which Justice Hawkes referred were Rules 14.37 and 14.48.
See also: Banerjee v.
Sood, 2024 ABCA 417 at paragraphs 14-18, and Spiess v.
Spiess, 2025 ABCA 3 at paragraphs 7-10.
Stay of a family law order In A.
K.
(H.), 2014 ABCA 361, 2014 CarswellAlta 1983, Justice Watson set out the test for granting a stay of a family law order.

His Lordship said, at paragraphs 17–21: 17 The test for an application for a stay of a family law order respecting custody and access to children is a modified version of the tripartite test for stays and injunctions pending appeal as set out in the decision of RJR-MacDonald Inc v Canada (Attorney General), [1994] 1 SCR 311:
(a) arguable case
(b) irreparable harm and
(c) balance of convenience.

18 The modification of the test in that context reflects the fact that, in such cases, the litigation is not a commercial dispute between adults or corporations, and the dominant consideration is the best interests of the children involved: see G(A) v J(J), 2008 ABCA 61 paras 11 to 12, 429 AR 394
MacPhail v Karasek, 2006 ABCA 320 para 3, 397 AR 305
B(C) v C(P), 2003 ABCA 321 para 4, 346 AR 121
S(CL) v S(BR), 2013 ABCA 349 paras 10 to 12, 37 RFL

The character of the modification includes the fact that the realities of such cases tend to blend all three of the criteria, or, put another way, the underlying facts tend to influence all three in a manner which is not the same as in disputes over money.
19 The modifications to the tripartite test, therefore, do not change the essential structure of the test, but they do influence the application of its elements.

In the first place, the first step of “arguable case” will likely be met by the existence of credible evidence that the best interests of any child involved have been impacted adversely in a significant manner by the order targeted by the proposed stay, coupled with the existence of an arguable case that the targeted order is flawed in some significant manner and that a stay would mitigate those adverse effects and better serve the best interests of the children: S(CL) v S(BR) at para 12.
20 This is a problematic area for child interests' cases.
That is because the child-centric modification thus involved is not intended to destroy finality as itself a key feature in the best interests of children.

While such an approach is manifested by notions of deference in appellate law, it is not desirable to subject the trial process to recurring (even tit for tat) efforts by parties to seek fresh opinions by different judges as a case proceeds through the courts.

Bastarache J in Van de Perre v Edwards, 2001 SCC 60 paras 11 to 13, [2001] 2 SCR 1014 included this: 13 … First, finality is not merely a social interest; rather, it is particularly important for the parties and children involved in custodial disputes.
A child should not be unsure of his or her home for four years, as in this case.
Finality is a significant consideration in child custody cases, maybe more so than in support cases, and reinforces deference to the trial judge's decision.
Second, an appellate court may only intervene in the decision of a trial judge if he or she erred in law or made a material error in the appreciation of the facts.
Custody and access decisions are inherently exercises in discretion.
Case-by-case consideration of the unique circumstances of each child is the hallmark of the process.

This discretion vested in the trial judge enables a balanced evaluation of the best interests of the child and permits [page1025] courts to respond to the spectrum of factors which can both positively and negatively affect a child.
21 The modification as to the first “arguable case” feature of the test has thus not been converted to a low standard of “any argument will do” merely because the interests of children are involved.

Cromwell JA, as he then was in Nova Scotia (Minister of Community Services) v F(B) and W(B), 20013 NSCA 125 para 13, 219 NSR 2d 67 explained that, “there will generally need to be circumstances of a “special and persuasive nature”, usually connected to the risk of harm to the children, in order to persuade the Court to grant a stay”.
In G.
G.

(R.T.), 2016 ABCA 186, 2016 CarswellAlta 1119, Madam Justice Schutz said: 21 The well-known test for a stay pending appeal as set out in RJR-MacDonald Inc v Canada (Attorney General), [1994] 1 SCR 311 at 334, 111 DLR
(4th) 385 is binding upon this Court.
The applicant has the burden of showing that:
(i) there is a “serious question to be tried” or, in other words, an arguable issue that is not frivolous and vexatious
(ii) there will be irreparable harm if the stay is not granted; and
(iii) the balance of convenience favours granting the stay.

22 The test is modified in a stay application dealing with parenting orders involving children, to reflect the paramount importance of the best interests of the child: B(C) v C(P), 2003 ABCA 321 at para 4, 346 AR 121; F(E) v S(JS)
(1995), 174 AR 296 at para 10; MacPhail v Karasek, 2006 ABCA 320 at para 3, 397 AR 305; G(A) v B(J), 2008 ABCA 61 at para 11, 429 AR 394.

The test has been described as being modified to require that, in addition to determining whether there is a serious issue to be argued on appeal that is neither frivolous nor vexatious, it is also necessary, in light of the best interests of the child, to consider from that perspective whether the child will suffer irreparable harm resulting from the granting or denial of the stay: Noel v Maj, 2006 ABCA 393 at para 3.
See also B(R) v P(D), 2007 PESCAD 19, 269 Nfld & PEIR 190.

23 As was said in CLS v BRS, 2013 ABCA 349 at paras 11–12: It is important to clarify that it is the best interests of the child or children which will have primacy in determining the balance of convenience, not the best interests of the parents.

The language in the test as read by the cases makes it clear that it is what the child or children would benefit from, not what the parents might benefit from—not necessarily what the father might like, or what the mother would like, or what their plans may be—that will influence what is in the best interests of the child.
Fundamentally the decision as to what the child or children's best interests are, ultimately, is of central importance in relation to an application for a stay.
I pause to note that the best interests of the children is a matter which impacts all three parts of the test.
To that extent, I agree with the sentiment of Macklin J. in Sopczak v.
Gye-Sik, 2011 ABQB 77 at para 10, 95 RFL

(6th) 338, where he also observed that “[w] henever courts consider the best interests of the child, there is a serious question to be tried.” … 27 When considering the second and third branches of the test for a stay, irreparable harm and the balance of convenience, the best interests of the child or children will determine the balance of convenience.
One has to look at the three parts of the test holistically, connecting irreparable harm with balance of convenience when little children are involved.
Those interests will ultimately determine the balance of convenience: CB v PC at para 4, EF v JSS at para 10: AG v JB, 2008 ABCA 61 at paras 11-12, 429 AR 394.
It is the “convenience” of the children that matters: EG v Alberta (Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act, Director), 2014 ABCA 237 at para 26.
There is a high evidential requirement on the applicant to prove irreparable harm: MacPhail v Karasek, 2006 ABCA 320 at para 3, 397 AR 305.
This was the test applied in E.T.T. v.
G.T., 2018 ABCA 279, 2018 CarswellAlta 2070.
In Jonzon v.
Yuill, 2020 ABCA 219, 2020 CarswellAlta 991, 10 Alta.
L.R.
(7th) 244, Justice Wakeling said (footnotes omitted): [2] The test for a stay of a child-custody or access order consists of three parts.
[3] First, has the applicant established that the likelihood the applicant will prevail on the appeal is high enough to justify the conclusion that the appeal is not frivolous or vexatious?
The court will not stay an original court's order if the prospects of a successful appeal are very low—hopeless or nearly hopeless.
[4] This part of the test is the same whether the stay is sought in the context of a commercial or a family law matter.

[5] Most of the time, an appeal court may allow an appeal “only if the original court's decision is the product of a misunderstanding of an important legal principle central to the resolution of the issue, or a factual determination that has no evidentiary basis … or an unfair hearing”.

[6] Second, has the applicant established that the child, or the applicant, will suffer irreparable harm if the stay is not granted. “‘Irreparable’ refers to the nature of the harm suffered rather than its magnitude.
It is harm which either cannot be quantified in monetary terms or which cannot be cured, usually because one party cannot collect damages from the other”.

[7] If the court concludes that the failure to grant a stay will cause the child irreparable harm, assuming that the applicant passes the other two parts of the test, the proper disposition is clear—issue a stay.

[8] If the court concludes that a stay will not cause the child irreparable harm, but will cause the applicant irreparable harm, the court should grant a stay, assuming that the applicant passes the other two elements of the test. … [10] The second element of the stay test has been modified to take into account the interests of the child or children.
This component does not work this way in commercial stays.
[11] Third, has the applicant established that the harm the child or the applicant will suffer if a stay is not granted exceeds the harm the child or the respondent will suffer if a stay is granted?
[12] Again, the traditional component has been revised to reflect the fundamental interest in the child's welfare.
In FG v.

KAV, 2020 ABCA 347, 2020 CarswellAlta 1740, Justice Antonio said: [8] The test for a stay pending appeal is set out in RJR-MacDonald Inc v Canada (Attorney General), 1994 CanLII 117 (SCC), [1994] 1 SCR 311 at 334.

The applicant has the burden of showing that i) there is a serious question to be tried, meaning there is an arguable issue that is not frivolous and vexatious; ii) there will be irreparable harm if the stay is not granted; and iii) the balance of convenience favours granting the stay.
[9] The three-part test is modified when dealing with a stay application involving a child, to reflect the paramount importance of the best interests of the child: CB v PC, 2003 ABCA 321 at para 4
CLS v BRS, 2013 ABCA 349 at paras 10–12
Bourgeois v Caldwell, 2017 ABCA 328 at para 7.
Analysis i)—Serious question [10] The threshold of whether there is a serious question to be tried is low.
The analysis does not require a detailed assessment of the merits of the case: CB v PC, supra at para 3.

Courts recognize that that there is often a serious question to be tried when the best interests of children are involved: CLS v BRS, supra at para 12, citing Sopczak v Gye-Sik, 2011 ABQB 77 at para 10
Bourgeois v Caldwell, supra at para 9.
However, just because the best interests of children are involved does not mean that “any argument will do”: DA v HK, 2014 ABCA 361 at para 21; Baker v Hunter, 2015 ABCA 309 at para 10.

An “arguable case” will likely be made out where there is credible evidence that the best interests of the child have been impacted adversely in a significant manner by the lower court's order, coupled an arguable case that the targeted order is flawed in some significant manner and that a stay would mitigate those adverse effects and better serve the best interests of the children: DA v HK, supra at para 19.

Due to the fact-based and discretionary nature of family law cases, and the desire to promote finality in family law litigation, considerable deference is given to a trial judge's findings: Hickey v Hickey, 1999 CanLII 691 (SCC), [1999] 2 SCR 518 at para 10

Spencer v Spencer, 2005 ABCA 262 at para 2. … ii)—Irreparable harm and balance of convenience [13] In Baker v Hunter, supra at para 11, the Court summarized the approach to the second and third parts of the modified test for a stay pending appeal as follows: The modified second and third parts of the test mandate a consideration of whether the children will suffer irreparable harm from the denial of a stay, and it is those interests that will ultimately determine the balance of convenience.

These parts of the test must be considered holistically, as irreparable harm is intricately connected with the balance of convenience when children are involved: AG v JB, 2008 ABCA 61 at para 12, 429 AR 394.

[14] Irreparable harm to the best interests of a child is not found in a mere disruption to a child's life: Noel v Maj, 2006 ABCA 393 at para 8; MacPhail v Karasek, 2006 ABCA 320 at paras 6–8; GR v CM, 2003 ABCA 268 at paras 17, 19.

Many cases distinguish between the words “practical” or “impractical” and “practicable” or “impracticable”.
Some do not.

Where distinction is made, it has been said that “practicable” has to do with something which is capable of being done, whereas “practical” denotes whether it can be done usefully or not at too great a cost: United Services Funds (Trustee of) v.
Richardson Greenshields of Canada Ltd.
Similarly, in Colonial Wood Packaging Inc. v.
Ontario (Ministry of Labour) (1991), 9 C.O.H.S.C.
91 at 96 (Ont.
Adjud.) Novick (Vice Adjudicator) stated that there is a distinction between “impracticable” and “impractical”, the latter being a word which connotes a lower standard.
Thus, to bring oneself under Rule 503(3)

(sic) [the reference should be to Rule 508(3)] where a different judge than from the one appealed from has entertained the stay application, and the stay application is attempted de novo before this court, if making the application to the judge appealed from was “impractical”, this court has de novo jurisdiction conferred upon it by Rule 508(3).

The onus of a party challenging that jurisdiction is to satisfy this court on that application that making the application for a stay to the judge appealed from was practical, or at least to lead some evidence that it was practical.
Then the onus may shift to the applicant to show that it was impractical.
Money Judgments If the judgment sought to be stayed is a money judgment, a two-part test (not the three-part test) seems to apply.
In Knelsen Sand & Gravel Ltd. v.
Harco Enterprises Ltd., 2021 ABCA 362, 2021 CarswellAlta 2716, Justice Wakeling explained how the tripartite test applies to money judgments.

His Lordship said (footnotes omitted): [34] There has been general agreement for the last fifteen years or so that the test for a stay of enforcement of a money judgment pending appeal is the tripartite test the Supreme Court has repeatedly endorsed—Harper v.
Canada, RJR-MacDonald Inc. v.
Canada, Quebec v.
143471 Canada Inc. and Manitoba v.
Metropolitan Stores (MJS) Ltd.
[35] Before 2000 some Alberta judges openly questioned the applicability of the tripartite test to money-judgment stays.
Justice Côté, in Alberta Provincial Judges' Association v.
Alberta, asserted that “[i]t is doubtful whether this three-part test applies to money judgments”.
The authors of the Civil Procedure Encyclopedia, of which Justice Côté is one, observed, “[h]ow irreparable harm can arise in a money case is unclear”.

Judges who favored a unique money-judgment stay test asked if there is “a special need for a stay, usually by showing that if the judgment were paid, the respondents would likely have trouble repaying it”.
[36] Judges who questioned the applicability of the tripartite test to money-judgment stays doubted the utility of the irreparable harm criterion.

[37] While the standard tripartite test is accepted today by Alberta courts as the norm governing all stay applications, it is fair to say that the tripartite test properly understood directs a court to address any legitimate concerns about the respondent's ability to repay any sum to which it is ultimately adjudged not to be entitled.
In doing so, it surely meets the concerns of those who were uncomfortable with the use of the standard test in assessing the merits of a stay of a money judgment.

Irreparable Harm In the course of deciding an application of a stay of a money judgment, Kerans J.A. made the following comments: In my view, one must take some care in the use of the expression “irreparable harm”.
I do not understand that the Metropolitan Stores case [Metropolitan Stores (MTS) Ltd. v.
Manitoba Food & Commercial Workers, Local 832, [1987] 1 S.C.R.
110] in the Supreme Court has offered any fresh definition of that term.
On the contrary, that decision merely reviewed the then-existing law.
Beetz J. did not attempt to offer any precise definition of the term.
In some contexts the term is used in this way: “irreparable harm not compensable in damages”, so that the expression contains its own definition.
You'll see that way of expressing it in injunction matters.
The meaning of “irreparable” turns on the nature of the application.
In the case of a stay of a money judgment, it seems to me, without more, there is always irreparable harm if a money judgment under appeal must be paid.

I say that because, not only is if the long practice of this Court to stay such judgments, but also it seems to me the sense of the matter in an application for a stay of execution of a money judgment.
Am I thereby undermining the irreparable harm test, to turn it into merely another expression of the balance of convenience test?
I think not.
Because I think there must be some demonstration of irreparable harm.
For example, if Mr.
Thompson today was able to produce shall we say a letter of credit or something of that sort in favour of the City, then I would refuse to make a stay because then there would be no irreparable harm.
But all Mr.
Thompson can promise me is that there's a strong likelihood that a judgment obtained by the City, if they're successful on their appeal, would be executed satisfactorily.
Well, the difficulty is, as counsel for the City replies, this offer raises all sorts of administrative and procedural issues.
For example, who is to say what the real estate is worth?
Is there a market?
Mr.
Thompson says his client owns real estate in the city worth several million dollars.
But you don't sell properties like that easily.
That is a highly specialized market.
It might take years.
A lot of things could happen.
I cannot accept the suggestion that consideration of those kinds of factors do not fall under the rubric of irreparable harm.
That is my view of the law, with the greatest of respect to those who take a different view.

I don't deny that there will be cases where the wealth of the respondent is so substantial and the liquid nature of the assets of the respondent so immense that these kinds of considerations pale into insignificance.
In this case, I'm afraid that I can't say that.
As a result, there will be an order for a stay.
Calgary (City) v.
Costello (1995), 31 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 159 (C.A.), at 161-62, per Kerans J.A.
In Moses v.
Weninger (2006), 55 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 37 (C.A.), Hunt J.A. discussed the concept of “irreparable harm”.
At p.
43, her Ladyship said: Irreparable harm refers to the nature, not the magnitude, of the harm.
Harm that is unquantifiable in monetary terms is irreparable.
Harm is irreparable where damages cannot be collected.

Impecuniosity is a relevant factor to consider but is not determinative … There can be irreparable harm if refusal to grant the stay renders the appeal nugatory. … Having to pay money alone is not irreparable harm. … Proof of irreparable harm may be shown where the amount of the judgment exceeds the ability of the ordinary citizen to repay. … In Prosper Petroleum Ltd. v.
Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Alberta, 2020 ABCA 85, 2020 CarswellAlta 368, 67 Admin.
L.R.
(6th) 15, 1 Alta.
L.R.
(7th) 1, Justice Strekaf said:
(23) It is recognized that irreparable harm will generally be established when a refusal to grant a stay might render an appeal nugatory: Knox v Conservative Party of Canada, 2007 ABCA 143 at para 17
Maverick Equities Inc v The Owners: Condominium Plan No 942 2336, 2008 ABCA 190 at para 11.
Is There a Serious and Arguable Ground on Appeal?

In the context, what must an appellant show to disclose a serious and arguable issue on appeal? … Central to a proper analysis of a finding on the first issue is the proper interpretation and definition of it.
In [Polansky Electronics Ltd. v.
AGT Ltd.
55 (C.A.)], Russell J.A., stated: The test for determining whether the appeal is arguable or not has a low threshold.

It does not require an examination of the merits of the case, but rather simply involves an assessment of whether the appeal is frivolous or vexatious … In support of this proposition, Russell, J.A., cited RJR-MacDonald Inc. et Imperial Tobacco Ltd. v.
Canada (Procureur général), [1994] 1 S.C.R.
In addition, in Triple Five Corp. v.
United Western Communications Ltd.
L.R.

(3d) 153 (C.A.), Kerans, J.A., of this court, in an application for a stay of an order vacating an interim injunction, stated at 155: Where it can be shown that the relief sought would be nugatory if a stay was not allowed and there is no harm to the respondent I have always granted a stay unless I can say that there was no reasonable possibility of success on the appeal.

Couching a serious and arguable issue on appeal in terms of whether the appeal is frivolous and vexatious or whether there is no reasonable possibility of success casts a low threshold on an applicant.

What seems clear from the cases is that it is perhaps unwise to attempt to define an exclusive and rigid meaning of “serious and arguable”, applicable to all cases. … I am persuaded that, in this case, the low threshold for a serious and arguable ground of an appeal is to be favoured, that is to say, is the appeal frivolous or vexatious or such that it has no reasonable possibility of success?
Integral Energy & Environmental Engineering Ltd. v.
Schenker of Canada Ltd.
360 (C.A.), at 363–364, per Wittmann J.A.
Interlocutory Orders Made in Trials The unusual aspect of this appeal is not that it is from an interlocutory order, but an interlocutory order made in the course of a trial.
Unlike other jurisdictions, Alberta by R.
508 permits an appeal, without leave, from an interlocutory order of a judge of the Court of Queen's Bench.
In jurisdictions where leave to appeal an interlocutory order must be obtained, the rule seems to be that leave is almost always denied where the order is made in the course of a trial.
A question arises about Alberta practice.
Appeals of this sort in civil cases are extremely rare, indeed one might say almost non-existent, at least in the recent past.
Novelty, of course, is no reason to refuse to hear an appeal.
The need to protect the due administration of justice, however, is such a reason.

This court can and should refuse to exercise its admitted jurisdiction to hear an appeal when to do so would suffer every trial to be delayed while each decision made by the judge in the course of a trial is the subject of a separate review.
In general, a party who feels aggrieved must await the final verdict.
Only then should this court review for possible error.
In our view, this system historically has proven to offer an adequate remedy for almost any injustice that might arise during the course of a trial.
In our view, the only exception to the general rule should be where the appellant can show that later review will not produce a just result.
Alberta Tank Ltd. v.
Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (1987), 53 Alta.
L.R.
And in another decision the Court of Appeal also said: We are all of the view that this court can refuse to hear an appeal when to do so is to abuse the judicial process.

The disruption to the trial process caused by appeals from interlocutory orders made in the middle of a trial is obvious and, except perhaps for the most unusual circumstance, this disruption is an abuse of process.
Any other rule would permit trials never to be finished.
Cascade Development Corp. v.
B.S.C.
Pension Fund Trustee Ltd.
L.R.
In Deloitte Haskins & Sells v.
Coopers & Lybrand Inc.
L.R.
(3d) 64 (C.A.), Madam Justice Russell, at pp.

68–71, analyzed a stay application (in respect of an interlocutory order) in the following manner: While the prima facie test no longer needs to be proven in private law matters, absent complexities similar to Charter issues, a preliminary assessment of the applicant's success on the appeal must be considered.
Since this is an interlocutory matter, the burden on the applicant is not as great as it would be if the matter had been finally disposed of at trial.
The ultimate rights of the parties will not be finally determined as a result of this application.
If the stay is not granted, the applicant may still proceed with its third party action, and may yet successfully defend the plaintiff's claim.
However, what the application must show is a potential for success both on the appeal and in the ultimate result.

The stronger the potential, the greater the likelihood that a stay will be granted, subject to a consideration of the other two factors … Harm is irreparable if it cannot be adequately compensated in damages. “Irreparable” refers to the nature of the harm, and not its magnitude: [RJR-Macdonald v.
Canada (Attorney General), [1994] 1 S.C.R.
311 at p.
341]… On the side of the applicant it is said that inconvenience to the plaintiff investors is minimal because the money is not at risk, although there will be a further delay in distribution.

The greater risk is that the applicant will be deprived of some right of recovery if the plaintiffs' action succeeds … On the side of the respondent it is said the inconvenience to the investment contract holders is substantial.
Many are elderly, and some are dependent upon these investments.
Some have died since the proceedings began, and the longer the distribution is delayed the greater the risk that more will be deprived of the enjoyment of these monies in their lifetime.
The prospect of individual hardship overshadows corporate loss.
I am reminded however, that financial hardship arising from a stay would be transient.

A stay would not foreclose substantive rights; the denial of a stay would … Considering the fact that the monies are not at risk if the stay is granted, and the possibility of an expedited appeal with terms that would mitigate prejudice to the plaintiffs, I find the greater harm would be suffered by the applicant if the stay is not granted.

Rule 14.48 Not Confined to Appeals from Queen's Bench In addition, it is perfectly clear under the Judicature Act and the Court of Appeal Act that the Court of Appeal still has all the general powers which the old Supreme Court of Alberta had.

The Court of Appeal Act specifically enables the Lieutenant-Governor-in-Council to make rules governing the practice and procedure of the court, and the Alberta Rules of Court were made under that power.
I cannot see anything in the portion of the Alberta Rules of Court dealing with appeals to the Court of Appeal which restricts all those Rules to appeals from the Court of Queen's Bench.
In particular, I cannot see anything which confines rule 508 to appeals from the Court of Queen's Bench.
Therefore it is my conclusion that under rule 508 I can consider the question of a stay of execution of a Development Appeal Board order appealed from.
Armstrong v.
Athabasca No.1 (County) (1990), 120 A.R.
Rule Only Applies to Appeals to Court of Appeal In Bourque v.
Tensfeldt, 2017 ABCA 236, 2017 CarswellAlta 1758, the Applicant sought an order staying enforcement of an order for costs made by a Master.
Justice Greckol dismissed the application on the basis that the Court of Appeal did not have jurisdiction to stay an order which was not being appealed to the Court of Appeal.
Her Ladyship said at paragraphs 5–6: 5 There is a preliminary issue regarding this Court's jurisdiction to stay enforcement of the Master's costs order of $5,500.
The costs order has not been appealed to this Court and, indeed, cannot be: r 14.4(4) of the Alberta Rules of Court, AR 124/2010, vol 1 [Rules].
The costs decision of the Master may be directly appealed to a justice of the Court of Queen's Bench: r 6.14(1).
6 Since Ms.
Bourque has not appealed, and cannot appeal, the Master's costs order to this Court, a single judge of this Court has no jurisdiction to stay its enforcement.
This Court only has the jurisdiction to stay enforcement of a decision pending appeal of that decision to this Court: r 14.48.
Accordingly, Ms.
Bourque's application for a stay of that order is dismissed.

Failure to Prosecute Appeal To get a stay fully intending to prosecute the appeal diligently, and then to fail to prosecute it would be bad enough … To get a stay not intending to prosecute the appeal diligently seems to me an abuse of process.
See Mireau v.
Saskatchewan (Minister of Justice), [1995] 4 W.W.R.
389 (Sask.
The English Court of Appeal says that counsel cannot ethically take instructions to file an appeal and then do nothing with it without telling that to the Court: Grosvenor (Mayfair) Estates v.
Raja, The Times, 2 Nov.
I can see some possible exceptions to that statement, such as a few weeks to get proper instructions.

But as a general principle, I agree with the English Court of Appeal … There are resemblances between an interlocutory injunction and a stay of execution pending appeal, and so much the same criteria apply to both: Metropolitan Stores (MTS) Ltd. v.
Manitoba Commercial Workers, Local 832, [1987] 1 S.C.R.
110 …RJR-MacDonald Inc. v.
Canada (Attorney General), [1994] 1 S.C.R.
311 …Frost v.
Assn. of Architects (Alberta) (1995), 30 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 93 (C.A.), at 96, per Côté J.A.
Mr.
Justice Côté referred to the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal decision in Mireau v.
Saskatchewan (Minister of Justice), [1995] 4 W.W.R.
In that case, the Saskatchewan court said at p.

391: When counsel goes on record for an appellant he thereby incurs an obligation to keep the matter moving by complying with the rules respecting the requisition of a transcript of the evidence (where applicable) but also any directions that the Court may make… This responsibility exists in both criminal and civil proceedings.
We adopt the reasons of Côté J.A. in R. v.
Van Le (November 25, 1994) (Alta.
C.A.
(Chambers)) (unreported) [now reported R. v.

4], in the following passages: I must point out that when counsel goes on the record for the appellant on a criminal appeal and gets bail for his client, he thereby incurs some very serious obligations to keep the matter moving.
Those obligations cannot be delegated, and if he wants to get out of them, he should apply to be relieved of them, or to have them extended, or to have himself taken off the record as counsel.
This is not the first time when the Court has seen an appeal move too slowly, though the appellant is on bail, when there has been a change of counsel.

That can not only slow things down, but leave the Court faced with a lawyer who is not the one who gave any undertakings or got the bail, in the absence of the lawyer who incurred those obligations and is ‘no longer acting’ in the matter.
This is not a correct understanding of the duties of counsel.
Unless and until the Court takes the obligations off the shoulders of the counsel who first incurred them, they remain on his shoulders.

If a second counsel comes along, that may add a second person with a duty, but it does not automatically remove the duty of the first one. … In circumstances where an appellant decides to take no further steps counsel should obtain instructions to immediately abandon the appeal, thereby saving unnecessary applications and consequent costs.
In Union Tractor Ltd. v.
Horseshoe Contracting Ltd.
L.R.
(4th) 33 (C.A.), Côté J.A., said, at pp.
35–36: An appellant who gets a stay of execution has an obligation to prosecute his appeal promptly and diligently.
That does not mean merely adhering to deadlines in the Rules. … It means taking each step so soon as is reasonably possible with due diligence.
It is no excuse that the appellant's counsel is a busy sole practitioner

Alberta is not short of lawyers. … There is nothing novel or obscure about that rule of law. … It is the practice of the Alberta Court of Appeal to grant stays of execution pending appeal only upon strict terms. … If there is no express term of the stay order, that duty of prompt prosecution is nevertheless implied.
If the appeal dawdles, the stay may be ended.
Appeal from a Denial of Stay In G.
Alberta (Family & Social Services) (1999), (sub nom.
S.G. v.
Alberta (Minister of Family & Social Services)) 237 A.R.
378 (C.A.), a single judge of the Court of Appeal had denied an application for a stay of proceedings pending appeal.
The appellant sought to have that denial reviewed by a three judge panel of the court.
At p.

380, the court said: We know of no provision for appeal to a panel of three judges from denial by a single judge of a stay of execution of judgment… We listened to S.G. only because his materials contained serious allegations of wrongdoing.
In no circumstances should this be interpreted to mean that this or a similar procedure to review the decision of a single justice of appeal acting under rule 508 has been approved by us.
Setting Aside a Stay Order In Dornan v.
Dornan Estate (2002), 98 Alta.
L.R.
83 (Alta.
C.A.
[In Chambers]) at p.
Russell J.A. then considered the question of who bore the onus on the application to set aside the stay.
She held that the onus fell on the party seeking to continue the stay.
At p.
33, she said: In Queen's Bench, the respondents sought a stay of the sale order.
Accordingly they bore the onus of establishing that the tripartite test for a stay was met.
In this court, it is the applicants who have applied for relief.
Ordinarily, the general rule that he who asserts must prove would suggest that the applicants bear the onus of proof before this court.
However, an application to this court under rule 508(3), subsequent to an application for a stay to Queen's Bench, is an application de novo.
Hence, this court must consider the matter afresh, as if it were being considered for the first time.
The onus is on the party seeking the imposition or continued imposition of the stay.
In Lausen v.

Alberta (Director of SafeRoads), 2022 ABCA 313, 2022 CarswellAlta 2489, Justice Ho gave this summary of the test to be applied on an application to set aside a stay (with an added comment on what to do when the stay order sought to be set aside was granted on consent of the parties): [12] On an application to set aside a stay, the court must consider the well-known tripartite test set out in RJR-MacDonald Inc v Canada (Attorney General), 1994 CanLII 117 (SCC), [1994] 1 SCR 311, 111 DLR
(4th) 385, but courts may also address additional factors, including delay, inequitable conduct, and policy considerations: Dreco Energy Services Ltd v Wenzel, 2008 ABCA 290 at para 27.

[13] A stay may be varied or set aside where there has been a change in circumstances, since it was granted, that would lead to a different assessment of one or more of the elements of the tripartite test: see Patel v Alberta (Securities Commission), 2019 ABCA 13 at para 11.
The circumstances of this application are, however, unique in that this stay order was entered into on consent and there is no record from the court below considering the tripartite test.
Regardless, I am able to consider factors such as delay and policy considerations which, in my view, are determinative of this application.
